content:
Hi folks,

This is an early announcement of things I have been working on and have been recently merged. I am writing about the ongoing work early, so that the community can possibly consider using these in near future. Basically, I have been working on improving the out-of-the-box experience with linters. I've done a couple of changes:

  • We now have an upstreamed version of batteries environment linters in Lean.Linter.EnvLinter.Basic. The main difference is that they are controlled using Lean.Option options. Each such linter needs to have an associated option, and this needs to be appropriately registered, for example:
public register_option linter.dummyMarker : Bool := {
  defValue := true
  descr := "(test) flag declarations whose name ends with 'DummyMarker'"
}
initialize addEnvLinterOption linter.dummyMarker

@[builtin_env_linter linter.dummyMarker]
public def dummyEnvLinter : EnvLinter.EnvLinter where
  noErrorsFound := "No dummy linter violations found."
  errorsFound := "DUMMY LINTER VIOLATIONS:"
  test declName := do
    if declName.toString.endsWith "DummyMarker" then
      return some "name ends with 'DummyMarker'"
    return none

Thanks to that, there is no need anymore to use nolints attribute, but rather you can just set an appropriate option. Also, one can define linter sets that contain environment linters and Lean.Linter linters.

  • For the user, the main entry point is lake lint --builtin-lint, which is a runner that displays all the collected Lean.Linter linter warnings and runs the environment linters. One can provide a flag --linters linter.linterOptionName1, linter.linterOptionName2, -linter.linterOptionName3 to specify which linters/linter sets they want to be turned on and off. Thanks to that, we can have linters that are turned off by default for the interactive mode, but are only ran in the batch mode. Of course setting flags will trigger a rebuild. There is also --lint-only flag that won't run the linters enabled by default, but only those specified.
  • There is a nice feature --record-exceptions that takes all the linter warnings and modifies the source files by setting an appropriate flag to false, rather than having to rely on the existing python script used in mathlib.
  • The full example of using new tool can be found here and here.
  • Environment linters, when working in module system mode do a public import rather than a private one (like batteries currently do).
  • Moreover, we now also have module linters, that is:
structure ModuleLinter where
  run : Array Syntax → CommandElabM Unit
  name : Name := by exact decl_name%

These receive a syntax of all top level commands of the module, but carry no info tree information.

  • I have also upstreamed a couple of mathlib/batteries linters to core, with some of them being disabled by default. impossibleInstance, nonClassInstance, simpVarHead, globalAttribute, modulesForbiddenWindows are now errors in core. defLemma (called now defProp), and checkUnivs are Lean.Linter linters enabled by default. unreachableTactic, unnecessarySeqFocus, dupNamespace and unusedDecidableInType are now upstreamed and disabled by default.

Also, in the near future, I am planning to work on stateful linters that can accumulate the information and can read other linters state. So, for example one will be able to have a dummy linter that incrementally computes some state and another one that reads it.

If you have any questions, I am more than happy to help. Just a heads up, for the next two weeks I will be away, but feel free to ping @Julia Markus Himmel.

Wojciech Różowski said:

  • There is a nice feature --record-exceptions that takes all the linter warnings and modifies the source files by setting an appropriate flag to false, rather than having to rely on the existing python script used in mathlib.

One thing that was nice about the old system is that we had two levels of ignores:

  • @[nolint foo], for recording "this linter is a false positive, please ignore it
  • nolints.json, for recording "this is something we need to fix, but haven't got around to yet.

Will the new system continue to support this two-tier approach?

I don't think this is really different from most other set_options that might appear in the code, so mathlib could decide to track this via a comment near the set_option line or invent some bespoke syntax to mark the intent of a set_option.
I suppose the ship somewhat sailed with the syntax linters not having this feature

This is very exciting! :tada:

I'm just curious, what exactly does exempting individual declarations with a set_option look like now if you don't have fine-grained access to the elaboration site? I'm wondering about two edge cases there:

  1. a command generates multiple declarations (e.g. structure) but we only want to turn the linter off for one of them
  2. we introduce a new env_linter downstream, and now want to exempt some upstream declarations

This is a good question. In general I think mathlib will want to declare the options for the environment linter seperately and put these declarations in Mathlib.Init, so that the linter can be disabled even if the linter isn't imported. I agree that this does not cover all cases. We might introduce syntax to disable environment linters on declarations after the fact.
Perhaps we can keep the nolint attribute machinery, but use real option names as keys?

Alternatively (just to brainstorm), the special syntax to disable environment linters after the fact could be based on set_option ... in (perhaps this is the intention behind that comment already?): something like set_option linter.unusedBaz false in linting my_foo_bar, or set_option linter.unusedBaz false for my_foo_bar (for instead of in, like deriving instance ... for).

(Hack: set_option linter.unusedBaz false in my_foo_bar could possibly be made to work by having set_option linter.* ... in specifically be its own special parser. But this might be bad for other reasons (namely, nothing else uses in this way).)

We're used to attribute management now, but I wonder if the goal is for that to completely disappear in the new linting UX for future users.
Indeed that could work, where linting is a command that just means "attach the current options as metadata to a declaration"
(though it would be a bit weird for linting to be valid as a standalone command)
True, I’m imagining there’d be a warning or linter against a standalone linting which explained its intended usage :)

Or maybe, against a standalone linting which appeared when no linter.* options were set? I guess one UX decision in this hypothetical would be to decide whether there’s enough of a use case for

-- disable linter for all these declarations
set_option linter.unusedBaz false

/- bunch of declarations -/

-- also these from elsewhere
linting my_bar_foo my_foo_bar …

or whether that nonlocality is just bad style and you shouldn’t do it.
As mentioned in #Lean Releases > v4.31.0 @ 💬 , it looks like maybe @[builtin_nolint] shipped after all?

I have a question about the checkUnivs linter, implemented in lean#13832: the nolints for this linter are different from the existing nolints in mathlib. Was there any difference in linter implementation, or did mathlib simply have some stale nolint entries? @Wojciech Różowski

Hey folks, sorry for a bit of the delay in replying, but I just got back from my vacation.

@Eric Wieser - builtin_nolint is currently not shipped in the latest nightly - it was something that I included initially, before implementing the option-based approach for enabling/disabling the linters, but it looks like the moment when 4.31 was cut, it was still there.

@Michael Rothgang - so basically, the logic of checkUnivs is the same and my first guess would be that those nolint entries are stale indeed.

Eric Wieser said:

Perhaps we can keep the nolint attribute machinery, but use real option names as keys?

This could be an option. I guess in such a setting local nolint would always trump more global option.
